meta.title: Who really said "Books will soon be obsolete in the schools"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Edison really said it — in a 9 July 1913 interview in The New York Dramatic Mirror. But the printed line reads "obsolete in the public schools."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Books will soon be obsolete in the schools'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: The New York Dramatic Mirror, 9 July 1913, page 24. Edison: "Books will soon be obsolete in the public schools." The short form drops a word.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1847–1931 · American inventor & pioneer of the motion picture
answer.sourceLine: Edison said it to a reporter, and it went into print on 9 July 1913. Frederick James Smith asked him what he thought motion pictures were worth to education, and Edison answered: “Books … will soon be obsolete in the public schools. Scholars will be instructed through the eye.” The attribution holds up exactly against the printed page — the only difference is that the familiar short form drops the word public (page 24 of the issue ↗).
answer.confidenceText: Verified — found on the printed page, where Edison says “in the public schools.”

source.heading: The interview, in print

docMeta.dd: The Evolution of the Motion Picture: VI – Looking into the Future with Thomas A. Edison
9 July 1913 — Vol. 70, No. 1803, page 24, column 3; by Frederick James Smith
Signed exclusive interview — the sixth in a series on the motion picture

source.excerpt: “What is your estimation of the future educational value of pictures?” I asked. “Books,” declared the inventor with decision, “will soon be obsolete in the public schools. Scholars will be instructed through the eye. It is possible to teach every branch of human knowledge with the motion picture. Our school system will be completely changed inside of ten years.”
trail: 9 July 1913 — the words appear in print for the first time, in Frederick James Smith’s interview on page 24 of The New York Dramatic Mirror: “Books … will soon be obsolete in the public schools” (Internet Archive scan ↗).

September 1913 — segments of the interview are reprinted elsewhere, including the Cleveland Plain Dealer and The State of Columbia, South Carolina. The Oregonian of 28 September prefaces the prediction with an apparently satirical “O joy!” and alters the wording to “instructed entirely through the eye” (Quote Investigator ↗).
16 December 1914 — The Syracuse Herald runs the line under the heading “‘Movies’ Vs. Books in Schools” and calls it a “disconcerting prophecy” (Quote Investigator ↗).

31 January 1986 — a Los Angeles Times article on the future of college education prints the version that became standard: “public” gone, a second “soon” added, “inside” deleted — the form in which the quote circulates today (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: Page 24, column 3, transcribed from the Internet Archive scan of the issue ↗. The same page reprinted the first two sentences as a display pull-quote in the sidebar: “Books will soon be obsolete in the public schools. Scholars will be instructed through the eye.”

author.metaLine: 1847–1931 · American inventor and businessman; pioneer of the motion picture
author.bio: Thomas Edison built the phonograph, the commercial incandescent lamp and much of the machinery of American motion pictures, and by 1913 was working daily at his laboratory in West Orange, New Jersey. He had a business interest in the prophecy he made here: his company was producing classroom films, and in the same interview he described reels on insects and chemical crystallization intended to make scientific truths “plain and clear to children.” He was wrong about the ten years, and made a similar forecast about textbooks again in 1922.

misattribution.heading: Right man, slightly wrong words
misattribution.intro: This is the unusual case: the famous name really did say the famous thing. What travels is a lightly worn-down version of it — a word missing here, a word added there, and in one prominent instance the wrong decade entirely.

items.why: The 1913 page reads “will soon be obsolete in the public schools.” Quote Investigator notes that in a Los Angeles Times article of 31 January 1986, “the word ‘public’ was omitted from this instance of the quotation, the word ‘soon’ was inserted a second time, and the word ‘inside’ was deleted” (Quote Investigator ↗).

items.scope: “Scholars will soon be instructed through the eye”
items.why: There is no second “soon” on the 1913 page: the sentence is simply “Scholars will be instructed through the eye.” The doubled “soon” appears in the 1986 Los Angeles Times version and again in a New York Times Magazine piece of 19 September 2010 (full text of the 1913 issue ↗).

A classroom-technology timeline in The New York Times Magazine of 19 September 2010 placed the remark in a “c. 1925” entry beside the filmstrip projector. Edison said it in 1913, and he was talking about motion pictures (Quote Investigator ↗).

“I believe that the motion picture is destined to revolutionize our educational system” is often merged into this one. It is a separate, later Edison statement, cited to Hugh Weir, “The Story of the Motion Picture,” McClure’s, vol. 54, November 1922, page 85 (Edison’s education predictions ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: the attribution is sound and the source is on the page — Edison said it in an interview printed 9 July 1913. Quote Investigator’s conclusion is that “Edison did make a statement in 1913 predicting the obsolescence of books in the public schools” and that “modern versions of Edison’s quotation are typically slightly altered” (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why he said it — and why it keeps getting quoted
lead: Edison was not idly speculating. The interview was the sixth in a Dramatic Mirror series on the future of the motion picture, and the man answering the questions had a stake in the answer: his company was already making what he called “school pictures.” In the very next breath he listed them — films of the fly, the mosquito, the silk-weaving moth, the gypsy moth, butterflies, chemical crystallization — which he said proved the worth of motion pictures in chemistry and physics, “making the scientific truths, difficult to understand from text books, plain and clear to children” (the printed interview ↗).

The line survives because it is the founding text of ed-tech scepticism: the most celebrated inventor alive, confidently wrong, on a ten-year deadline. Newspapers were sceptical almost immediately — a Syracuse paper filed it in December 1914 under “disconcerting prophecy” — and a century on it is still the standard reply to classroom-technology hype. When the U.S. Education Secretary and the FCC Chairman promoted laptops for every schoolchild in 2012, a Los Angeles Times columnist reached straight for it (Quote Investigator ↗).
context.detailsSummary: What else Edison predicted that afternoon
detailsBody: He was asked whether talking pictures would kill the silent photoplay. “I do not think so,” he answered. “Both will be used.” He pulled a strip of colour film from his pocket, called it raw but said natural-colour photography “is going to come,” and expected stereoscopic films with the effect of actual depth. He also thought few homes would own a projecting machine, “although the wealthier people will possess them, no doubt” (The New York Dramatic Mirror, 9 July 1913 ↗).

Edison did not let the idea go. A later statement — “I believe that the motion picture is destined to revolutionize our educational system” — is cited to Hugh Weir, “The Story of the Motion Picture,” McClure’s, vol. 54, November 1922, page 85. It is a separate quotation from a separate source, and is frequently blended with the 1913 one (Konrad M. Lawson, Edison’s education predictions ↗).
